In the spring of 1903 the harbor commission of Alder Cove, a fishing port of nine hundred people, met to settle a question it had deferred for six years. Hollis Vane, the engineer the town had hired the previous autumn, laid his plan before the seven commissioners: to cut a second entrance through the sand spit at Low Point, so that vessels need not beat around the shoal in a southerly wind. His estimate was fourteen thousand dollars, more than Alder Cove had ever borrowed at one time. When the meeting opened, the standing motion was the merchant Amos Kerr's, to do the work in stages over ten years and borrow nothing. Two commissioners, Pell and Danforth, had said nothing at all.

What moved them was neither Vane's drawings nor his figures. A letter came from an Army engineer at the district office, undertaking to match, dollar for dollar, whatever Alder Cove itself spent on the cut. Fourteen thousand dollars had suddenly become seven, and Pell and Danforth voted with Vane that evening.

Kerr's answer was not that the work was useless. It was that the district office had given two other towns the same undertaking within his memory and had honored it in neither of them. He lost, five to two, and the town borrowed in June.

The town dug its own half of the cut in 1904 and stopped. The federal money arrived in 1912 and came to less than a third of the sum promised. The entrance was opened to nine feet and never to the fifteen Vane had drawn; vessels used it in fair weather and avoided it in foul. Whether it would have answered at full depth cannot be said. Vane left in 1908 for a larger post, and the minute book gives the whole business one line.

Fishermen have called it the camanchaca for as long as anyone can remember: a fog thick enough to soak a shirt, thin enough to see the sun through. It carries no rain. The village of Aguada, four hundred meters below the ridge, receives less than fifteen millimeters of rain a year and has no river, so for a century its water arrived by truck. In 2019 a research station on the ridge strung forty nets of fine polypropylene mesh across the fog's path. For six seasons Ines Marchetti followed grey chatterbirds through the thorn scrub of the eastern Karoo, and for six seasons one habit refused to make sense. Chatterbirds keep a piercing two-note call for hawks alone; when it sounds, every bird within earshot drops flat or dives into cover, and nobody forages for a minute or more. Yet Marchetti's notebooks filled with hawkless alarms — three hundred and forty of them, by her own count, with nothing overhead but cloud.

Her first thought was ordinary error: a shadow, a startled dove, a bird jumping at nothing. But mistakes ought to be scattered evenly through a group, and these were not. Sixty-nine percent of the hawkless calls came from whichever bird had taken the sentinel perch above the group, the one spot from which the whole foraging party can be watched, and a sentinel has the least excuse for mistaking a shadow.

What followed the calls was just as lopsided. Marchetti filmed fifty-eight hawkless alarms at close range. In forty-one of them the caller dropped from its perch within seconds and carried off the item a startled neighbour had let fall — usually something bulky: a scorpion, a hairless mouse, a beetle grub too fat to swallow whole.

Correlation is not proof, so in her fifth season Marchetti set out to make the alarms happen. On alternate mornings she baited the feeding stations either with slivers of meat that go down in a gulp or with whole scorpions, which a bird must beat and dismember in the open. Marchetti now calls the hawkless alarm a lie told for a mouthful: a signal meaning hawk, given by a bird that eats when everyone else believes it. What she cannot explain is why the lie still works.
